  gender: Female
  ethnicity: South Eastern Asian
  relationship_status: Single

  trauma_type: Captivity
  pcl5: 74

Patient-reported symptoms:
  Threat: Startle to Movement: Unexpected movement nearby causes me to react as if I am in danger, Back to Wall: I feel unsafe unless my back is against a wall where I can see the room, Intrusion Monitoring: I listen for sounds that might mean someone is entering my home
  Negative Appraisals: Self-Blame: The event happened because of the way I acted, No Accountability: The people responsible have faced no consequences, Body Shame: I feel ashamed of what happened to my body

Vignette:
Mai Tran was twenty-five when she was taken. She had been working late at the tax consultancy firm in downtown San Jose, finalizing a client’s quarterly filings, and the office had emptied around her. She remembered the exact moment she looked up from her screen and saw that the cleaning crew had already come and gone, leaving the floor polished and silent. She had thought nothing of it—she often worked late. But on her way to the parking garage, a man had stepped out from the stairwell door and pressed something cold into her ribs. She had not screamed. She had done exactly what he said. That was what she could not stop turning over in her mind: the way she had complied, the way she had not fought, the way her voice had stayed small and cooperative even as he shoved her into the back of a van. For three days, she had been held in a storage unit on the edge of the city. She had been bound, blindfolded, and left in the dark. She had not seen her captors’ faces, but she had heard their voices—calm, unhurried, discussing her as though she were a piece of inventory. They had been caught eventually, but the charges had not stuck. Mai had learned this from a detective’s voicemail, left on a Tuesday afternoon, the words clinical and flat: insufficient evidence, case closed. No one had faced anything. No one had answered for what happened to her body.

In the months that followed, Mai’s life began to narrow. She had always been careful—meticulous, her colleagues called it—but now careful was not enough. She had to be vigilant. She started sitting with her back to the wall in every restaurant, every meeting room, every coffee shop. If she could not find a seat that allowed her to see the entire space, she would leave. She had come to believe that her survival depended on knowing where every exit was, on never being caught unaware again. At home, she slept only after checking every lock twice, and even then, she lay awake listening. She listened for footsteps in the hallway, for the click of a key in the lock, for the sound of breathing that was not her own. She had begun to monitor the silence itself, straining for the smallest noise that might mean someone was entering. It was exhausting, but she was certain that if she stopped, she would be taken again.

At work, her colleagues noticed she had grown jumpy. A hand on her shoulder from a manager made her flinch so hard she knocked a cup of coffee across her desk. She began to avoid the break room, where people moved unpredictably, and she stopped using the elevator after a man stepped in too close behind her. She told herself it was just preference, but she knew the truth: she could not tolerate unexpected movement nearby without her body flooding with adrenaline, her heart hammering as though she were back in that dark, cold space. She started arriving early and leaving late, not out of diligence but to avoid the crowded hallways. Her productivity did not suffer—she was still sharp with numbers—but her relationships frayed. She stopped accepting invitations to after-work drinks. She stopped explaining why.

What brought Mai to therapy was not the fear itself, but the shame. She felt ashamed of what had happened to her body during those three days, though she could not say exactly why. The shame sat in her chest like a stone, and it made her want to disappear. She had not told anyone the full story—not her mother, not her closest friend from college. She was afraid that if they knew, they would see her the way she saw herself: someone who had done something wrong, someone who had caused her own captivity by the way she had acted. She had gone over it a thousand times. If she had left at six instead of nine. If she had taken the elevator instead of the stairs. If she had screamed. The logic was circular, but it did not loosen its grip. In the waiting room of the clinic, she sat with her back to the wall, her hands folded in her lap, listening to the footsteps in the hallway. She wanted to stop being afraid. But more than that, she wanted to stop being ashamed. She wanted to believe that what had happened was not her fault. She was not sure she could.
